title: A Change Is as Good as a Rest
description: Entertainment, travel and the language of a holiday told afterwards: the words of leisure (canoeing, harbour cruising, hiking, roller skating, safari, sightseeing, sky diving, sunbathing, surfing, water skiing), of accommodation (a cottage, a terraced house, a spacious en suite apartment, a tent, a resort) and of the services a hotel and a room offer, from ironing and baby-sitting facilities to a car park and a 24-hour laundry service; the coastline lexis of the module (bay, cave, cliff, creek, harbour, lagoon, path, reef, shoreline, wreck, crystal clear) and the feelings a holiday leaves behind, from excited, enthusiastic and hopeful to disappointed, regretful and fed up; comparatives and superlatives, with the short and the long adjectives, the irregular good, bad and far, the modifiers much, far, a lot and a bit that English puts in front of a comparative and the very it refuses, and the in and the of that follow a superlative; the prepositions of place and of movement that a route needs (along, across, through, around, into, out of, off, at, on, in); the past perfect against the simple past, its form had plus a past participle, the earlier of two past events, the before and after that already fix the order and the case the book itself sets aside, two actions so close in time that the past perfect is not usually used; the WH words and the information each one asks for; the linkers of a letter of complaint, from Unfortunately, To start with and Added to this to Last but not least, with the difference between a conjunction that takes a whole clause and a preposition that takes a noun; the three-part plan of that letter, its layout blocks, the register a stranger is written to and the look forward to that is followed by an -ing form; the language of a survey report, from none of us to nearly all of us; and the vowels of the module, where the same spelling hides four different sounds
